assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Sparking
items.clue: A sudden flow of charge across a gap.

items.label: Non-contact force
items.clue: Acts between two things that are not touching.

questions.stem: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other one.
Rubbing creates fresh charge on the surface of each material.
Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.
Electrons are rubbed off both materials into the nearby air.

questions.explanation: This is the specification's own account: negatively charged electrons move from one material on to the other, leaving the giver positive and making the receiver negative.

questions.stem: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps across a gap to a nearby earthed metal pipe. Why does the spark happen?

options.text: Air can never conduct, so the light must come from the metal pipe.
Charge can only cross a gap at the moment two surfaces touch.
The charge on the object grows heavy enough to fall across.
The field grows strong enough for the air in the gap to conduct.

questions.explanation: As charge builds up, the electric field across the gap grows. Once it is strong enough the air stops insulating and charge flows across, which is the spark.

questions.stem: Which of these is the definition of the density of a material?

options.text: The volume the sample fills divided by its own mass.
The mass of the sample multiplied by the volume.
The mass of the sample divided by its volume.
The total mass the sample happens to have.

questions.explanation: This is the definition the specification gives: density = mass / volume.

questions.stem: A sealed container holds 200 g of ice. The container is left until all the ice has melted. What does the balance read now?

options.text: 200 g, because melting rearranges the particles but removes none.
Less than 200 g, because some of the ice gets used up as it melts.
More than 200 g, since liquid water is denser than solid ice.
100 g, since the water takes up far less room than the ice.

questions.explanation: Mass is conserved in a change of state. The container is sealed, so nothing can enter or leave.

questions.stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What has happened to the cloth?

options.text: It has gained some protons from the rod, so it is positively charged.
It has lost electrons to the rod, so it is now positively charged.
It has lost all of its charge, so it now has no charge at all.
It has made new positive charge on its surface while rubbing.

questions.explanation: The rod became negative by gaining electrons, and those electrons came from the cloth. Losing electrons leaves the cloth with an equal positive charge.

options.text: A set of paths that a charged object has to follow.
A region in which a charge experiences a force.
Only the lines drawn around a charge on a diagram.
The charge that has built up on a rubbed object's surface.

questions.explanation: A charged object creates a field around itself, and a second charged object placed anywhere in that region feels a force.

questions.stem: In the equation ρ = m/V, what do the symbols m and V stand for?

options.text: m stands for mass and V stands for volume.
m stands for metres and V stands for volume.
m stands for mass and V is the speed it moves.
m stands for the weight and V for the volume.

questions.explanation: These are the quantities the specification lists for this equation: mass, m, in kilograms and volume, V, in metres cubed.

questions.stem: Solid carbon dioxide sublimates in an open dish on a balance and the reading falls to zero. Has any mass been destroyed?

options.text: Yes, subliming uses the solid up, so that mass has gone for good now.
No, but gases weigh nothing at all, so the reading had to fall away.
Yes, because a gas is a new substance made out of that solid.
No, the gas has spread into the room and is not on the balance.

questions.explanation: Sublimation is a change of state, so mass is conserved. The balance reads zero only because the carbon dioxide is no longer on the pan.

questions.stem: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material always equal in size to the negative charge on the other?

options.text: Rubbing always produces equal amounts of the two charges at once.
Both of the materials are rubbed with exactly the same steady force.
Every electron lost by one is an electron gained by the other.
Charge always spreads out evenly between the two materials.

questions.explanation: The two charges are the two sides of one transfer, so counting electrons on either side must give the same number.

questions.stem: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change as you move further away from the sphere?

options.text: It gets stronger, because the field spreads out as it goes out.
It stays the same up to the last line and then stops there.
It stays exactly the same all around the charged sphere.
It gets weaker; the field is strongest close to the charged sphere.

questions.explanation: The specification states it directly: the field is strongest close to the object and the further away you go, the weaker it is.

questions.stem: Which unit does the specification use for density?

options.text: kilograms times metres cubed, kg m³
kilograms per metre squared, kg/m²
kilograms per metre cubed, written kg/m³
grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³

questions.explanation: The specification gives density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3, which follows from dividing a mass in kg by a volume in m^3.

questions.stem: Why is boiling water classed as a physical change rather than a chemical change?

options.text: Steam is a new substance, but a very easy one to turn back.
Physical changes are reversible and chemical changes are not.
Boiling can be undone, so it cannot be a chemical change.
The steam is still water; cooling gives the liquid back.

questions.explanation: In a physical change no new substance is formed, and reversing the change recovers the original properties.
